concepts.def: Studies internal mental processes such as perception, memory and thinking by inference from behaviour.
Mental framework for organising knowledge; aids efficient processing but distorts memory (Bartlett 1932).
Mind seen as an information processing system with input, encoding, storage and retrieval stages.
Drawing conclusions about unobservable mental processes from observable behavioural data.
Combines cognitive psychology with brain imaging (fMRI, PET) to map mental functions to neural structures.
Diagrammatic representations of mental processes, e.g. multi-store model, working memory model.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Cognitive Psychology — a core area of A-Level Psychology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Cognitive Psychology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Cognitive Psychology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Studying internal mental processes by inference from behaviour is the:
options: Behaviourist approach
Cognitive approach
Biological approach
Humanistic approach

mcqs.q: Which neuroscience method maps brain activity using blood oxygenation?
options: EEG
fMRI
CT
X-ray

mcqs.q: Why does the cognitive approach use INFERENCE?
options: Because brain scans are unreliable.
Internalisation of group beliefs.
Because cognitive psychologists guess instead of measuring.
Mental processes cannot be directly observed, so they are inferred from behaviour.
